He was previously a meditation trainer, and the Lotus part was named for the sitting position for meditation. He eventually—and famously—stepped down during his amazing success from the CEO role at Lotus 1-2-3 because he reportedly did not enjoy the lifestyle of a CEO. I heard about this newfangled Lotus 1-2-3 program and convinced the CEO to buy me a computer so I could try to automate the tracking spreadsheets. I fell in love with that program and quickly had built a digital version of the real estate firm’s financial spreadsheets. The result, as you certainly know now, was that changing a number only took a few seconds and the entire spreadsheet was updated automatically. The chief financial officer of that company thought it was magic. As an aside, many years later, after Mitch Kapor had retired and started a small fund with his wife, I was raising money to start the company where I worked with Nass and Reeves from Stanford on a human–computer interface for online customer support automation. While I knew this was not a fit for Mitch and his wife’s fund, I asked for and got a meeting to show it to him. The office was tiny, with none of the pomp and circumstance of high-end funds. When I arrived, he was in his office on the phone and paused to tell me to set up in the conference room, and he would be right there. “But don’t use the TV on the stand,” he told me. “That is my wife’s, and she just got it, and I don’t want to screw it up.” I couldn’t help myself. After a few minutes in the conference room, I banged two metal chairs together and then quickly poked my head into his office and said, “Mitch, I broke the TV.” He told the person on the phone he would call them back and hung up. When he came around the corner to see the TV fully safe and unharmed, I told him I was kidding. We both had a good laugh. I proceeded to tell him that my business idea was not a fit but that he was one of my heroes and I’d just wanted to meet him. I told him the story of automating the books at the real estate company. I just wanted him to know that his work had a big impact on my life, and to say thank you. It was a real highlight for me to sit and chat with him for the next hour. But back to our exploration here. For the short run and for many jobs, anyway, I believe the statement goes like this : AI is not coming for your job. Someone who knows how to use AI is. Soon, we will explore a potential longer-term reality of a world with AI with the ability to do most jobs as we bring this all together. But in the short to medium term, in many jobs, I tend to believe that there will be great prosperity for those who learn to use AI to radically increase their productivity. There can be no doubt that after I upgraded the real estate company to digital spreadsheets, the accounting department got much smaller. However, by plugging in, I ended up being promoted when I was near college graduation; after several years of working for the firm while going to college, the CEO made me a vice president of that company and put me in charge of my own development projects. You simply have to plug in to stay relevant. Certainly, there will be jobs that will simply whole cloth be replaced by AI in a fairly short time frame. For example, a call center representative. This is a job that can already be done better and far cheaper by an AI voice agent trained on the company policies and given access to its customer records. For those folks, I would think now is the time to begin to train yourself on AI to do something else productive, but it very likely will not be what you are currently doing. But overall, during the short to medium term, I suspect you will see two distinct company profiles of leveraging AI and a continuum between the two. At very large and mature companies with relatively modest growth rates and deep market penetration, you will see a strong push to drive cost out of the business using AI. But for medium to small businesses with high growth rates and low market penetration, meaning lots of space to grow faster, I believe you will see a real push to accelerate growth with AI enhancements and much less attention to removing cost. At my learning company, Amplifire, we have plans to go department by department and job by job in 2026 to deploy AI into the hands of our team and make them three to ten times more productive. Let me explain why I think this split will occur. If a company can grow at a high rate with high margins, the rewards are extraordinary. It’s called the Rule of 40. You take the growth rate (say 20 percent) and the profit rate (say 20 percent) and add them together to get a desired Rule of 40. And this is one of the key metrics that drives the enterprise value of the company. It is often a trade-off between the two. To grow faster, you spend more on marketing and sales, for example, before you see the results. Now imagine, with AI, you could grow at 35 percent but have margins of 35 percent because of leveraging AI in the hands of your team rather than hiring more people.
